hero.sub: There's an order beneath the chaos — in data, in markets, in people. My job is to find it.

when.label: WHEN YOU NEED ME
items: You have data, but no clear answer for why things turned out the way they did.
The more stakeholders involved, the slower everything gets — and something always gets lost.
You move fast, but when things break, there's no one to own the fix end-to-end.
A campaign underperformed and you're not sure why — or how to prevent it next time.

items.title: Finding a $200K creator in a 3,000-follower channel
items.desc: Platform sales data revealed Tesla accessories were outperforming — leading to a creator discovery that broke every assumption about follower count.
items.context: AliExpress Korea's influencer group-buying operates on a CPS (Cost Per Sale) model — commissions are paid based on sales performance, with no upfront fees. Actual sales conversion, not channel size, is the core criteria for partner selection.
items.problem: Subscriber count indicates reach, but does not correlate directly with purchase conversion. Follower-based channel selection showed low predictive accuracy, and cases of small channels outperforming large ones were repeatedly observed. A quantifiable framework for evaluating sales potential in advance was needed.
items.role: Contribution: ~95%. End-to-end ownership — channel discovery, data tracking, outreach, and contract structure design.

approach.intro: Shifted the channel selection criteria from follower count to the density of purchase-intent audiences. Three indicators were used to evaluate channels.

steps.title: Inbound Data Tracking
steps.desc: Identified YouTube channels that had reviewed AliExpress-listed products, then tracked actual platform inflow and purchase conversion data through links in video descriptions.

steps.title: Community Engagement Pattern
steps.desc: Channels that communicated directly with followers through separate channels (e.g., open KakaoTalk chats) tended to attract prospective buyers rather than passive content consumers.

steps.title: Content Purpose
steps.desc: Channels focused on delivering information and deals — rather than entertainment — showed higher viewer-to-buyer conversion rates.

approach.outro: Applying these criteria, a Tesla accessories channel with approximately 3,000 subscribers was identified. Meaningful sales contribution was pre-confirmed through link tracking data, and the community engagement pattern matched the target profile.

items.result: Average GMV per campaign: $200K+. Equivalent to the output typically seen from channels with 100K+ subscribers. The same discovery framework applied to a running shoe channel (also several thousand subscribers) produced consistent results of $200K+ per campaign.
items.lesson: Follower count is an indicator of reach, not conversion. Purchase behavior is determined by the type of audience a channel attracts — not its size. Viewers who come for information and deals behave differently from those who come for content. This framework was applied to subsequent category expansion (automotive accessories) and produced repeatable results.
items.improvement: The discovery criteria remained personal know-how rather than a formalized scoring system. While insights were shared in team review sessions, a standardized evaluation framework was never documented — which limited scalability across the team.

items.title: 18 hours to resolve a full-order cancellation
items.desc: A human error triggered a total order cancellation on a 2.8M-subscriber creator campaign. Resolved in 18 hours. Industry standard: 7–14 days.
items.context: In June 2025, a co-branded group-buying campaign was planned and executed involving Intel, Itsub, and AliExpress. Itsub is a tech YouTuber with 2.8M+ subscribers — a high-opportunity, high-risk partnership where any negative experience for followers could directly translate into brand damage.
items.problem: At midnight on the final day of the one-week campaign, all orders were converted to a full cancellation. The cause was a human error: the 'cancel all orders if sales target is not met' option had been left active during event setup. As the cancellation triggered, viewer complaints began flooding the comments section of the creator's channel.
items.role: Contribution: ~90%. Led the full response — incident recognition, internal reporting, solution design, stakeholder coordination, direct user communication, and drafting and approving the public notice. Final decisions were made with approval from the Korea General Manager and team lead.

approach.intro: Three tracks were executed in parallel immediately upon identifying the incident.

steps.title: Internal Reporting and Decision-Making
steps.desc: At 1 AM, the situation was reported to the team lead, department head, and Korea GM. The creator was also informed in real time. The resolution direction converged quickly under a single principle: customer experience first — all affected buyers would be given the opportunity to repurchase at a price lower than the original.

steps.title: Emergency Budget Approval and Re-setup
steps.desc: The original payment discount budget had expired with the event's close. An emergency budget request was submitted, and re-setup began immediately upon approval.

steps.title: Direct User Communication
steps.desc: A dedicated inquiry inbox was opened for direct responses. Comments on the YouTube video were addressed one by one. Responsibility was clearly attributed to AliExpress to prevent backlash from being directed toward the creator.

approach.outro: The public notice was drafted, refined with GPT assistance, and submitted for urgent review to Legal and PR teams — who responded despite it being the weekend. Final approval was obtained before publishing.

items.result: From incident recognition to final public notice: under 18 hours. The same type of incident typically takes 7–14 days to resolve internally. The creator responded positively to the speed of response and the measures taken to protect followers. The campaign concluded without lasting brand damage.
items.lesson: Human error is an inevitable byproduct of complex manual setup processes. Following this incident, a double-check protocol for critical option values was introduced to the event setup workflow.
items.improvement: Response speed was fast, but approximately 30 minutes were spent assessing the situation alone before reporting. The more efficient sequence would have been to report immediately and conduct the assessment in parallel.

items.title: 3–4 years of data, one screen, zero budget
items.desc: Campaign data sat in scattered Excel files for years. Built a dashboard using an internal tool nobody used — no dev resources, no directive.
items.context: Three to four years of influencer group-buying campaign data was stored across individual Excel files. Retrieving performance data for a specific campaign or tracking cumulative creator contribution required manually opening and consolidating multiple files each time — an inefficient structure that created unnecessary friction in decision-making.
items.problem: The data existed but was not usable in its current state. Repeated analyses — campaign performance comparison, creator contribution tracking — were being done manually every time. A solution was needed that required no new tool procurement or development resources.
items.role: Contribution: 100%. Problem identification, tool selection, data cleaning, dashboard design, and build — all completed independently. A self-initiated project, started during overtime without any external directive.

approach.intro: An underutilized dashboard feature within an existing internal tool was identified. It was implementable without development resources, and work began immediately. The project was executed in three stages.

steps.title: Data Collection and Integration
steps.desc: Distributed Excel files were consolidated into a single data source. Inconsistent formats and creator name variations across files were standardized under a unified schema.

steps.title: Data Cleaning
steps.desc: Creator name discrepancies, missing values, and duplicate entries were resolved manually. Input format standards were established to ensure future data would accumulate consistently.

steps.title: Visualization
steps.desc: A dashboard was built around the most frequently needed metrics: GMV by campaign, cumulative contribution by creator, and performance by category.

items.result: Manual retrieval and consolidation for campaign performance and creator contribution tracking was replaced by a single dashboard view. The tool saw active internal use until AI agent-based workflow automation became more widely adopted.
items.lesson: The value of data is maximized through cleaning and structuring, not collection alone. If the format in which data is recorded is not standardized, even the best analysis tools will fail to deliver usable output. This project confirmed that standardizing data entry is a prerequisite for any analytics infrastructure.
items.improvement: No formal onboarding was provided to the team after the dashboard was built. Knowing a tool exists and actually using it for decision-making are different things — closing that gap should have been part of the rollout.

items.desc: As AliExpress's official Olympic partner, traveled to Paris with Korean creators — the first time the platform brought influencers together offline at this scale. It was a business trip. But what I remember most isn't the numbers.
To mark the 11.11 Global Shopping Festival, coordinated 30+ influencer teams to Alibaba HQ in Hangzhou for on-site shoots — handling visas, logistics, and local escorts. All of it for the first time.
